title: Linear Programming Using Limited-Precision Oracles
contribution: Shows that, under mild assumptions, polynomially many calls to a limited-precision LP oracle plus polynomially many bit operations suffice to solve an LP exactly, as theory for the exact-LP methods that work best in practice (IPCO version; abstract).
problem_entry: Exact LP over the rationals through an oracle that returns limited-precision solutions; earlier work assumed oracles of arbitrary specified precision, polynomial but at a precision the abstract calls often unrealistic for practical computation (abstract).
key_idea: Treat the practical solver as a limited-precision LP oracle; under mild assumptions, a polynomial number of oracle calls and of bit operations computes an exact LP solution (abstract).
assumptions: LPs solved exactly over the rational numbers; the oracle returns limited-precision LP solutions; the mild assumptions behind the result are not spelled out in the abstract (abstract).
proof_devices: Oracle-complexity framing: count oracle calls plus bit operations instead of assuming arbitrary precision (abstract)
experiments: Not in the abstract (the journal version S029 reports SoPlex experiments, card c09).
positioning: Against earlier analyses that assume oracles of arbitrary specified precision; claims a foundation for the methods currently most effective in practice for exact LP (abstract).
writing: The abstract states the prior assumption, calls its precision unrealistic, then sets the new result against it (abstract).
limits_future: Not stated in the abstract, which also does not name the practical methods the theory explains (per the S029 card, iterative refinement with basis verification or rational reconstruction; inferred).

method_links.note: The limited-precision producer is taken as given and only the exact work is counted: the producing/deciding split as a complexity question (IPCO abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: oracle model of the production solver
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an oracle capable of returning limited-precision LP solutions stands for the practical solver (IPCO abstract; existing candidate from S029)

transferable: To analyse a practical numerical method, give the floating-point solver a precision contract (a limited-precision oracle), then count oracle calls plus exact bit operations instead of assuming arbitrary precision (abstract).
coauthors: Daniel E. Steffy; Gleixner first of two (Crossref)

quotes.text: Under mild assumptions, it is shown that a polynomial number of calls to such an oracle and a polynomial number of bit operations, is sufficient to compute an exact solution to an LP.
a foundation for understanding and analyzing the behavior of the methods that are currently most effective in practice for solving LPs exactly

title: On generalized surrogate duality in mixed-integer nonlinear programming
contribution: Revisits surrogate (constraint-aggregation) relaxations for MINLP, generalizes them to several simultaneous aggregations and gives the first algorithm for the best set of aggregations, with experiments on dual-bound strength (IPCO version; abstract).
problem_entry: MINLP relaxations are usually required to be convex, but current solvers handle a moderate presence of nonconvexities, which opens the door to tighter nonconvex relaxations (abstract).
key_idea: Use the nonconvex surrogate relaxation, studied for linear integer programs in the 1970s-80s and scarcely since, in an MINLP setting; generalize it to multiple aggregations at once and give the first algorithm that computes the best set of aggregations, with computational enhancements (abstract).
assumptions: MINLPs; the relaxation may be nonconvex because current solvers can handle a moderate presence of nonconvexities (abstract).
proof_devices: First algorithm that computes the best set of aggregations, with computational enhancements; details not in the abstract (abstract)
experiments: Extensive computational experiments on the strength of the dual bounds; test set, solver and numbers not in the abstract (abstract).
positioning: Revives surrogate relaxations, actively studied for linear integer programs in the 1970s-80s and scarcely considered since (abstract).
writing: Argues from a solver capability (handling moderate nonconvexity) to the choice of a dormant relaxation, and names benefits and challenges together (abstract).
limits_future: Says it shows computational challenges as well as benefits; which ones is not in the abstract. A MINLP paper, outside this team's MILP field (team.json gives MINLP to minlp-team).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: revive a dormant classical relaxation once solvers can handle it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: surrogate relaxations, studied for linear IPs in the 70s and 80s and scarcely since, are revisited because current solvers handle a moderate presence of nonconvexities (IPCO abstract)

transferable: When solvers gain a capability (here, handling moderate nonconvexity), look again at classical relaxations that need it, even if they have been dormant for decades (abstract).
coauthors: Benjamin Müller (first), Gonzalo Muñoz, Maxime Gasse, Andrea Lodi, Felipe Serrano; Gleixner fourth of six (Crossref)

quotes.text: These relaxations were actively studied for linear integer programs in the 70s and 80s, but they have been scarcely considered since.
present the first algorithm that is capable of computing the best set of aggregations

title: Accelerating domain propagation: An efficient GPU-parallel algorithm over sparse matrices
contribution: A domain-propagation algorithm whose rounds run entirely on the GPU, with geometric-mean speed-ups of about 10x to 20x (up to 180x) on large instances (journal version; abstract of the arXiv preprint 2009.07785).
problem_entry: Propagation of linear constraints is crucial in MIP and pseudo-Boolean solvers, but dynamic behaviour, dependency structures and sparsity make parallel and GPU implementations hard; the abstract names this as a main reason why propagation in state-of-the-art solvers is single-threaded (abstract).
key_idea: An algorithm that avoids these irregularities, runs efficiently on GPUs and executes whole propagation rounds on the GPU without CPU synchronization or communication (abstract).
assumptions: Linear constraints of MIP and pseudo-Boolean problems over sparse matrices (title; abstract).
proof_devices: Propagation rounds run entirely on the GPU, with no synchronization or communication with the CPU (abstract)
experiments: On state-of-the-art GPUs, geometric-mean speed-up about 10x to 20x for reasonably large instances, up to 180x on favourably large ones; baseline, instances and hardware not in the abstract (abstract).
positioning: Against single-threaded propagation in state-of-the-art solvers (abstract).
writing: The two design properties are listed as (a) and (b); the speed-up is stated per instance-size class (abstract).
limits_future: Not stated in the abstract; the later S077 abstract reports the parallel version even more competitive in a real-world setting than first reported (S077 abstract). The journal's own abstract was not reachable (no Crossref or OpenAlex abstract; ScienceDirect HTTP 403); the ZIB OPUS journal record gives five bullet points (by their form, the article's highlights) that repeat these claims (metadata).
transferable: Design a parallel propagation so that complete rounds run on the GPU with no CPU synchronization or communication (abstract).
coauthors: Boro Sofranac (first), Sebastian Pokutta; Gleixner second of three (Crossref)

quotes.text: This is one of the main reasons why domain propagation in state-of-the-art solvers is single thread only.
on state-of-the-art GPUs, our geometric mean speed-up for reasonably-large instances is around 10x to 20x and can be as high as 180x on favorably-large instances

title: An algorithm-independent measure of progress for linear constraint propagation
contribution: An algorithm-independent measure of progress for iterative linear-constraint propagation, applied to premature termination on real-world MIP instances and to a GPU-versus-sequential comparison (journal version; abstract).
problem_entry: Tolerance-based stopping criteria make fair efficiency comparisons of iterative propagation codes difficult, and unbounded variable domains make the relative size of reductions hard to quantify (abstract).
key_idea: Measure, independently of the algorithmic design, the progress an iterative propagation procedure has made at a given point of its run (abstract).
assumptions: Bounds propagation of linear constraints in MIP solvers; iterative algorithms with tolerance-based stopping; unbounded variable domains in the formulation (abstract).
proof_devices: Progress measure defined independently of the algorithmic design, applicable at any point of a run (abstract)
experiments: (i) How far heuristic stopping criteria terminate prematurely on real-world MIP instances; (ii) a GPU-parallel propagator against a sequential state-of-the-art implementation, the parallel one even more competitive in a real-world setting than originally reported (abstract).
positioning: Against tolerance-based stopping criteria that make implementations hard to compare fairly (abstract).
writing: Two numbered questions of practical relevance, (i) and (ii), in the abstract itself (abstract).

method_links.note: A comparison problem the field handles with tolerances becomes a defined measure, then answers two practical questions; SKILL.md cites the CP version [CP21] for this (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: progress measured independently of the algorithmic design (journal abstract; existing candidate from D003)

transferable: Before comparing iterative codes that stop at different tolerances, define a progress measure that depends on neither algorithm and compare them on that scale (abstract).
coauthors: Boro Sofranac (first), Sebastian Pokutta; Gleixner second of three (Crossref)

quotes.text: However, these heuristic stopping criteria can pose difficulties for fairly comparing the efficiency of different implementations of iterative propagation algorithms in a real-world setting.

(ii) We compare a GPU-parallel propagation algorithm against a sequential state-of-the-art implementation and show that the parallel version is even more competitive in a real-world setting than originally reported.

title: A computational status update for exact rational mixed integer programming
contribution: Revises the 2013 hybrid-precision exact MIP framework (symbolic presolve, exact repair of heuristic solutions, an iterative-refinement rational LP solver, verifiable certificates) and reports a 10.7x average speedup and 2.9 times as many solved MIPLIB 2017 benchmark instances (journal abstract).
problem_entry: The last milestone in roundoff-error-free solving of general MIPs over the rationals was the hybrid-precision branch and bound of Cook, Koch, Steffy and Wolter (2013); the paper starts from that framework (abstract).
key_idea: Revise and extend the 2013 framework: symbolic presolving, an exact repair step for solutions from primal heuristics, a faster rational LP solver based on LP iterative refinement, and independently verifiable certificates of optimality (abstract).
assumptions: General MIPs over the rational numbers, solved roundoff-error-free; MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set (abstract).
proof_devices: Exact repair step for solutions from primal heuristics (abstract)
Rational LP solver based on LP iterative refinement (abstract)
experiments: MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set, two-hour limit: 10.7x average speedup over the original framework and 2.9 times as many instances solved (journal abstract); the IPCO abstract (D002) gives 6.6x and 2.8 for the same comparison and neither explains the change. Floating-point baselines are not in the abstract.
positioning: Continues the Cook, Koch, Steffy and Wolter (2013) framework, named as the last milestone (abstract).
writing: Opens by naming the last milestone with authors and year, then lists the four additions in one sentence (abstract).

method_links.note: The predecessor milestone is named, its missing components are added one by one, and the gain is measured against it (journal abstract).
The framework produces independently verifiable certificates of optimality (journal abstract).
Exact repair of heuristic solutions and a rational LP solver built on LP iterative refinement (journal abstract).

transferable: Give an exact solver an exact repair step for the solutions that its inexact primal heuristics find (abstract).
coauthors: Leon Eifler (first); Gleixner second of two (Crossref; ZIB and HTW Berlin per the first-page check of the open PDF)

quotes.text: The last milestone achievement for the roundoff-error-free solution of general mixed integer programs over the rational numbers was a hybrid-precision branch-and-bound algorithm published by Cook, Koch, Steffy, and Wolter in 2013.

We describe a substantial revision and extension of this framework that integrates symbolic presolving, features an exact repair step for solutions from primal heuristics, employs a faster rational LP solver based on LP iterative refinement, and is able to produce independently verifiable certificates of optimality.

title: Efficient separation of RLT cuts for implicit and explicit bilinear products
contribution: Detects bilinear products hidden in MILP constraints with binary variables and separates RLT cuts only from constraint/bound-factor combinations expected to be violated, evaluated in two solvers (IPCO version; abstract).
problem_entry: RLT gives tight linear relaxations of nonconvex continuous and mixed-integer problems; the paper widens its reach for bilinear products and attacks the high cost of RLT cut separation, named as one of the major difficulties in practice (abstract).
key_idea: (1) Detect bilinear product relations implicit in MILPs by analysing linear constraints with binary variables; (2) a separation algorithm that picks combinations of linear constraints and bound factors expected to yield an inequality violated by the current relaxation solution (abstract).
assumptions: Nonconvex continuous and mixed-integer problems with bilinear products; implicit products found in MILPs through linear constraints with binary variables (abstract).
proof_devices: Detection of implicit bilinear products from linear constraints with binary variables (abstract)
Separation that selects constraint/bound-factor combinations expected to yield a violated inequality (abstract)
experiments: A detailed computational study based on implementations in two solvers; the abstract names neither the solvers nor numbers (SCIP and Gurobi per the S070 card) (abstract).
positioning: Extends RLT, a prominent relaxation technique, to a new class of problems and targets its separation cost (abstract).
writing: Two contributions, numbered in the abstract: detection first, separation second (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: independent re-implementation in a second solver as replication
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the computational study is based on implementations in two solvers (IPCO abstract; existing candidate from S070)

transferable: Before generating cuts from a large family, select only the factor combinations predicted to give an inequality violated by the current relaxation point (abstract).
Evaluate a new solver component through implementations in two different solvers (abstract).
coauthors: Ksenia Bestuzheva (first), Tobias Achterberg; Gleixner second of three (Crossref)

quotes.text: First, a method for detecting bilinear product relations implicitly contained in mixed-integer linear programs is developed based on analyzing linear constraints with binary variables, thus enabling the application of bilinear RLT to a new class of problems.

We propose a new RLT cutting plane separation algorithm which identifies combinations of linear constraints and bound factors that are expected to yield an inequality that is violated by the current relaxation solution.

title: Investigating Round-Up Properties for the Length-Constrained Cycle Partition Problem
contribution: Builds small counterexamples to IRUP for the set-partitioning formulation of the length-constrained cycle partition problem and gives simple sufficient conditions that explain IRUP on 30 of 51 benchmark instances (abstract).
problem_entry: The set-partitioning formulation of LCCP, solved by branch and price, consistently has IRUP on standard benchmark instances; the paper studies when that property holds (abstract).
key_idea: Construct counterexamples with small coefficients in which the formulation lacks IRUP, and give simple conditions under which IRUP holds (abstract).
assumptions: Partition a graph's nodes into as few cycles as possible, with no cycle longer than the critical time of any of its nodes; set-partitioning formulation solved by branch and price; standard benchmark instances from the literature (abstract).
experiments: The conditions explain IRUP on 30 of the 51 standard test instances that have it; 21 remain unexplained (abstract; the 21 by subtraction).
positioning: Starts from an empirical regularity on standard benchmark instances from the literature (abstract).
writing: Defines IRUP inline in one clause (abstract).
limits_future: A partial explanation: 21 of 51 instances with IRUP are not covered (subtraction from the abstract); no future work stated. By topic part of the LCCP line that SKILL.md's Method 3 traces ([LCCP24] to [LCCP26]; inferred).

method_links.note: An observed regularity is checked per instance and counted (30 of 51), but the belief concerns a formulation's property rather than solver behaviour, and the check is a sufficient condition, not a per-decision check of a solver run (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: counterexample plus sufficient condition, coverage counted on the benchmark
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: small-coefficient counterexamples to IRUP, simple sufficient conditions, and the share of benchmark instances they explain (30 of 51) (abstract)

transferable: When a formulation shows a property on every benchmark instance, build small counterexamples to show it is not guaranteed, derive simple sufficient conditions, and report how many benchmark instances the conditions explain (abstract).
coauthors: Kilian Runnwerth (first), Mohammed Ghannam; Gleixner last of three (Crossref)

quotes.text: On standard benchmark instances from the literature, this formulation consistently satisfies the integer round-up property (IRUP), i.e., the objective value of the root node relaxation rounded up is equal to the optimal objective value.
Our computational tests reveal that 30 out of 51 standard test instances with IRUP can be explained by these conditions.
